The strongest underfollowed candidates are small-cap AM names rather than traditional defense primes. The key policy-linked hypothesis is that NDAA/CRMN-style qualification and restrictions on China/Russia additive equipment could shift demand toward US/allied printer, materials, software, and inspection ecosystems, but later layers must verify budget authority, contract conversion, balance-sheet runway, and whether defense revenue is material versus marketing language. Layer 1B expansion found a small set of US-listed public companies plausibly tied to defense-qualified additive manufacturing bottlenecks: metal AM equipment and qualified production capacity, AM metal powders, and secure/vetted distributed manufacturing infrastructure. The strongest underfollowed angle is not generic 3D-printing demand, but qualification, ITAR/CMMC/AS9100 controls, metal-powder process consistency, and defense-acceptable supplier networks.
